paras: The attempted lynching of James Sergeant took place on the night of August 11, 1920, in Hoboken, New Jersey, when a crowd beat Sergeant, a Black man of 21, and chased him into a motion picture theatre shouting "Lynch him!" Police held the crowd off with drawn revolvers until reserves arrived, and Sergeant was taken to headquarters and charged with disorderly conduct. New York dailies reported it the next day under headlines about a lynching averted, and the Chicago Whip carried a short report a week later.

Sergeant lived at 352 Newark Street in Hoboken, near John Peterson, whose address the Evening World and the Tribune gave as 358 Newark Street. Earlier that evening Peterson reported to police headquarters that Sergeant had insulted his wife, whom the Sun named as Mrs. Josephine Peterson and described as a white woman. According to the Tribune, police advised him to wait until morning and apply for a warrant, and the Sun wrote that he went home "evidently dissatisfied."

Accounts of how the attack began differ: the Evening World said a fight started between Peterson and Sergeant, the Tribune that a dozen men stopped Sergeant near his home and beat him, and the Sun that a crowd caught him at Newark and Clinton streets. Sergeant broke away and ran two blocks to a motion picture theatre at First and Grand Streets, with a growing crowd behind him. The Sun said the pursuers shouted "Lynch him!" as he ran into the theatre.

Patrolman Joseph Holmes stood in the lobby with a drawn revolver and, by the Sun's account, threatened to shoot the first man who tried to enter. Bernard M. McFeely, Hoboken's director of public safety (the Tribune called him police commissioner), sent in a riot call and, with Lieutenant James Lavezzo, drew his revolver and ordered the crowd to disperse. When the crowd kept demanding Sergeant, reserves came, and the Evening World reported that police used clubs on a score or more of men before getting him away. McFeely was bruised on the head and body in the fighting.

Sergeant was taken by patrol wagon to police headquarters, where a cordon of police kept back a crowd that was "still uttering threats." A surgeon dressed his injuries, including a deep cut over his eye, and the Petersons made a formal complaint at the station. Sergeant was held for disorderly conduct, or in the Tribune's wording for disturbing the peace, and was to be arraigned on August 12. No report of the arraignment's outcome or of any arrest among the crowd was found.

Three New York papers ran the story on August 12, each with its own estimate of the crowd: "more than five hundred" in the Sun and New York Herald, 1,000 in the New-York Tribune and almost 2,000 in the Evening World. Their headlines centered the police rescue, such as the Sun's "NEGRO ESCAPES 500 HOBOKEN LYNCHERS" and the Tribune's "Police Reserves Rescue Negro From Mob," while repeating the accusation as the cause, as in the Tribune's "Beaten for Insult to Woman." The Evening World put the injured official in its subhead, "Director of Safety Badly Battered as He Joins in Fight to Save Negro."

The Chicago Whip printed a brief front-page dispatch from Hoboken on August 21 under the headline "POLICEMAN HURT REPELLING MOB." It called the crowd "a mob of more than 2,000 men and women" and said Sergeant was "beaten into insensibility before he was rescued." Unlike the white dailies, the Whip did not mention an insult and said he was attacked because Peterson's wife "had shown a preference for him."

The white dailies gave Peterson's complaint of an insult as the cause, while the Chicago Whip attributed the attack to his wife's preference for Sergeant, without naming a source. Estimates of the crowd ran from more than 500 to more than 2,000, and the Whip described heavier injuries than the Sun's bruises and cut over the eye.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of James Sergeant
bases: A crowd pursued and beat Sergeant and tried or threatened to lynch him, shouting 'Lynch him!', until police drove it back (A1, A3, A4, A6).

A crowd of hundreds to thousands acted without authority to punish Sergeant for an alleged insult to a white woman, but police rescued him alive, so no one was killed (A1, A4, A6); it was an attempted lynching.
Three New York dailies and the Chicago Whip independently report the pursuit, beating and police rescue of Sergeant, differing mainly on crowd size and cause (A1, A2, A4, A6).
